title: Iraq after Saddam
subtitle: 2003–today · The Occupation and the Dissolved State, the Sectarian Civil War, ISIS and the Ruin of Mosul, the Muhasasa Order and the Iranian Ascendancy, the Tishreen Uprising, and the Unfinished Country

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The occupation and the CPA, the new political order and the muhasasa quota, the Maliki years and the authoritarian drift, ISIS and the war for the cities, the post-ISIS governments and the Tishreen shock, the Sadrist movement, the Iran-backed militias, and the Kurdistan Region

entries.label: The occupation and the CPA
entries.hint: The Coalition Provisional Authority under Paul Bremer governed Iraq for fourteen months and made two decisions that shaped everything after: the sweeping de-Baʿthification of May 2003, which purged the state of its experienced managers, and the dissolution of the Iraqi army, which put half a million armed and humiliated men on the street. There was no plan for the aftermath, and the aftermath arrived at once.
entries.note: George Packer, 'The Assassins' Gate: America in Iraq' (2005); Ali Allawi, 'The Occupation of Iraq: Winning the War, Losing the Peace' (2007).

entries.label: The new political order
entries.hint: A constitution ratified in 2005 set up a parliamentary federal republic in which every office and contract is shared out by ethnic and sectarian quota — the muḥāṣaṣa. Power settled with a coalition of Shia Islamist parties and the two Kurdish parties; the Sunni Arabs, boycotting at first, came back weakened. Every election since has produced the same horse-trading and a government months in the forming.
entries.note: Toby Dodge, 'Iraq: From War to a New Authoritarianism' (2012); Fanar Haddad, 'Understanding Sectarianism' (2020).

entries.label: The Maliki years and the authoritarian drift
entries.hint: Nuri al-Maliki, prime minister for eight years, drew the security services, the courts and the money into his own hands, ran a sectarian security policy that treated Sunni areas as enemy territory, and answered the Sunni protest movement of 2012–13 with force — the Hawija killings, the closed camps. When ISIS swept out of Syria in 2014 it found, in the alienated Sunni north, a population that would not fight for Baghdad.
entries.note: Toby Dodge, 'Iraq: From War to a New Authoritarianism' (2012); Emma Sky, 'The Unravelling' (2015).

entries.label: ISIS and the war for the cities
entries.hint: In June 2014 a few thousand ISIS fighters took Mosul as four Iraqi divisions dissolved. A caliphate was declared over a third of the country. Sistani's call to arms raised the Popular Mobilisation Forces — mostly Iran-linked Shia militias — and with a US-led air campaign the cities were retaken one by one: Ramadi, Fallujah, and finally Mosul in a nine-month battle in 2016–17 that levelled its old city. Victory was declared in December 2017.
entries.note: Joby Warrick, 'Black Flags: The Rise of ISIS' (2015); the reporting of the Mosul campaign in the ICG and UNHCR briefings.

entries.label: The post-ISIS governments and the Tishreen shock
entries.hint: After ISIS the politics resumed its old rhythm — Abdul-Mahdi, then a caretaker under Kadhimi, then Sudani from 2022 — but the ground had shifted. In October 2019 a mass youth uprising, Tishreen, rejected the entire post-2003 order; the state and the militias killed some six hundred protesters and the Abdul-Mahdi government fell. The demands for reform were not met, and the same parties held on.
entries.note: the ICG reports on the Tishreen movement; Faleh A. Jabar's posthumous analyses; Renad Mansour on the post-2018 order.

entries.label: The Sadrist movement
entries.hint: Muqtada al-Sadr inherited his father's mass following in 2003 and turned it into a militia — the Mahdi Army, which fought the coalition at Najaf and in Sadr City — and then the largest single bloc in parliament. Populist, unpredictable, Iraqi-nationalist and hostile to both Washington and Tehran, he storms the political stage and walks off it by turns; his followers stormed parliament in 2016 and again in 2022.
entries.note: Patrick Cockburn, 'Muqtada: Muqtada al-Sadr, the Shia Revival, and the Struggle for Iraq' (2008).

entries.label: The Iran-backed militias and the PMF
entries.hint: A cluster of Shia armed groups — the Badr Organisation, Asaʾib Ahl al-Haq, Kataʾib Hezbollah and others, most tied to Iran's Revolutionary Guard — fought the Americans, then ISIS, and were folded into the state in 2016 as the Popular Mobilisation Forces while keeping their own commands, funds and foreign policy. They hold ministries, border crossings and seats in parliament: a state within the state.
entries.note: Renad Mansour & Faleh A. Jabar, 'The Popular Mobilization Forces and Iraq's Future' (Carnegie, 2017).

entries.label: The Kurdistan Region
entries.hint: The Kurdistan Regional Government entered the new Iraq as a going concern and boomed through the 2000s on oil and its own stability — Erbil rising, foreign consulates, an airport. Then came the ISIS war on its doorstep, the oil-price crash, and the 2017 independence referendum, which Baghdad answered by retaking Kirkuk and its oil. The region kept its autonomy and lost its momentum, and the old KDP–PUK split hardened.
entries.note: Gareth Stansfield & Mohammed Shareef (eds.), 'The Kurdish Question Revisited' (2017); David Romano on the referendum.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The insurgency and al-Qaeda in Iraq, the sectarian civil war and the cleansing of Baghdad, the war against ISIS, the Yazidi genocide at Sinjar, the Tishreen uprising and its suppression, and the US–Iran shadow war on Iraqi soil

entries.label: The insurgency and al-Qaeda in Iraq
entries.hint: Within months of the invasion a Sunni insurgency — former officers, nationalists, and the foreign jihadists of Abu Musab al-Zarqawi's al-Qaeda in Iraq — was killing coalition soldiers and, deliberately, Shia civilians. Fallujah was fought over twice in 2004, the second time flattened. Zarqawi's strategy was to provoke a sectarian war, and in 2006 he got one.
entries.note: Ahmed Hashim, 'Insurgency and Counter-Insurgency in Iraq' (2006); Joby Warrick, 'Black Flags' (2015).

entries.label: The sectarian civil war
entries.hint: The bombing of the Shia shrine at Samarra in February 2006 set off eighteen months of sectarian slaughter: death squads on both sides, bodies in the Tigris, the ethnic cleansing of Baghdad's mixed neighbourhoods into Sunni and Shia zones. At the peak some three thousand Iraqis were killed a month. It ebbed after 2007 with the US troop surge and the Sunni tribal Awakening against al-Qaeda.
entries.note: Nir Rosen, 'Aftermath: Following the Bloodshed of America's Wars in the Muslim World' (2010); the Baghdad demographic studies.

entries.label: The war against ISIS
entries.hint: The three-year campaign to destroy the caliphate combined the Counter-Terrorism Service, the rebuilt army, the Kurdish peshmerga, the Popular Mobilisation militias and a US-led coalition air force. It retook Tikrit, Ramadi and Fallujah and then, in a grinding nine-month fight, west Mosul — much of the historic city reduced to rubble, thousands of civilians killed, a million displaced.
entries.note: the UN and Amnesty reporting on the Mosul battle; James Verini, 'They Will Have to Die Now: Mosul and the Fall of the Caliphate' (2019).

entries.label: The Yazidi genocide at Sinjar
entries.hint: When ISIS overran the Sinjar region in August 2014 it set out to exterminate the Yazidis as devil-worshippers: men and older boys shot into pits, thousands of women and girls enslaved and sold, tens of thousands besieged on Mount Sinjar. Around five thousand were killed and six thousand taken; a large part of the community fled abroad. The UN recognised it as genocide, and thousands are still missing.
entries.note: the UN Human Rights Council report 'They Came to Destroy: ISIS Crimes Against the Yazidis' (2016).

entries.label: The Tishreen uprising and its suppression
entries.hint: In October 2019 hundreds of thousands of young Iraqis — mostly Shia, from the very heartland of the ruling parties — filled the squares of Baghdad and the south demanding jobs, services, an end to the quota system and to the militias, and an end to Iranian influence. The security forces and militia gunmen answered with live fire and targeted assassinations; some six hundred were killed. The government fell; the system did not.
entries.note: Human Rights Watch and Amnesty reporting on the 2019–20 protests; the ICG briefing 'Iraq's Tishreen Uprising' (2021).

entries.label: The US–Iran shadow war on Iraqi soil
entries.hint: Iraq became the ground on which Washington and Tehran fought their contest: rocket and drone attacks by Iran-linked militias on US bases and the embassy, US strikes back, and in January 2020 an American drone at Baghdad airport killed Qasem Soleimani of the Revolutionary Guard and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis of the PMF. Parliament voted to expel US forces; they stayed, reduced. The attacks and reprisals continue.
entries.note: the reporting on the Soleimani strike and its aftermath; Ranj Alaaldin and others on the militia–US dynamic.
keywords: Qasem Soleimani of the Revolutionary Guard
Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis of the PMF

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The muhasasa system, the 2005 constitution and the federal question, the security sector and the militias, the oil-rentier state at its maximum, the Shia religious authority and the state, and the Kurdistan Region as a semi-state

entries.label: The muhasasa quota system
entries.hint: Every ministry, agency, provincial post and public contract is shared out among the ethnic and sectarian blocs in rough proportion to the last election — the muḥāṣaṣa. Each bloc runs its ministries as a private fief, staffs them by patronage, and takes its cut. Nobody is accountable to the voter, because the outcome is fixed before the vote. It is the machine that produces the corruption, the paralysis and the anger, and it has proved unreformable from within.
entries.note: Toby Dodge, 'Iraq: From War to a New Authoritarianism' (2012); Renad Mansour & Christine van den Toorn, 'The 2018 Iraqi Federal Elections' (2018).

entries.label: The 2005 constitution and the federal question
entries.hint: The constitution written in 2005 under Kurdish and Shia pressure made Iraq a federation, entrenched the Kurdistan Region, left the 'disputed territories' including Kirkuk to a referendum under Article 140 that was never held, and promised an oil-and-gas law that has never passed. It settled the shape of the state on paper while leaving its hardest questions — who owns the oil, where the internal borders run — permanently open.
entries.note: the Iraqi Constitution of 2005; Jonathan Morrow, 'Iraq's Constitutional Process II' (USIP, 2005).

entries.label: The security sector and the militias
entries.hint: The monopoly of force is fragmented. There is a rebuilt army that collapsed in 2014 and was rebuilt again; an effective special force, the Counter-Terrorism Service; a federal police; and the Popular Mobilisation Forces — dozens of militias, many Iran-linked, made a legal state body in 2016 but keeping their own chains of command, budgets and agendas. The state does not fully control the men with guns who act in its name.
entries.note: Renad Mansour, 'Networks of Power: The Popular Mobilization Forces and the State in Iraq' (Chatham House, 2021).

entries.label: The oil-rentier state at maximum
entries.hint: Oil provides over ninety per cent of the government's revenue and about ninety-nine per cent of its exports. The state employs some four million people as patronage, subsidises fuel and electricity it cannot supply, and raises almost nothing in tax. There is no productive private economy to speak of. It is the rentier condition in its purest form: a government that distributes a windfall and answers to no one for how.
entries.note: the World Bank Iraq Economic Monitor reports; Ahmed Tabaqchali on the Iraqi budget.

entries.label: The Shia religious authority and the state
entries.hint: Ali al-Sistani, the senior marjaʿ at Najaf, holds no office and rarely appears, but he has been the decisive arbiter of the new Iraq. He forced the occupation to hold elections; his 2014 fatwa raised the army that stopped ISIS; his withdrawal of support in 2019 brought a government down. It is a quietist authority — guidance, not rule, the implicit opposite of the Iranian model — and it keeps proving stronger than the politicians.
entries.note: Robert Gleave, 'Conceptions of Authority in Iraqi Shiʿism' (2007); Sajjad Rizvi on Sistani; the Najaf–Qom debate literature.

entries.label: The Kurdistan Region as a semi-state
entries.hint: The Kurdistan Region has its own government, parliament, armed forces, oil policy, tax collection, immigration control and foreign representation. It exports oil through Turkey against Baghdad's wishes, argues over its budget share every year, and split between a KDP zone and a PUK zone with separate administrations. It is a federal unit that functions as a state, and the friction with the centre never resolves.
entries.note: Gareth Stansfield, 'The Islamic State, the Kurdistan Region and the Future of Iraq' (2014); the annual Baghdad–Erbil budget disputes.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Shia ascendancy and the shrine-city revival, sectarianism institutionalised and then contested, the Sunni Arabs' predicament, and the minorities' catastrophe

entries.label: The shrine cities revived
entries.hint: With the Sunni political monopoly gone, Najaf and Karbala came into the open. The seminaries grew, the shrines were rebuilt and re-gilded, and the pilgrimage exploded: the Arbaʿīn walk to Karbala, on which some twenty million people converge on foot each year, is now the largest annual gathering on the planet. Religious tourism became a pillar of the southern economy and the atabat the working heart of world Shiism.
entries.note: the Arbaʿīn pilgrimage statistics; Elvire Corboz, 'Guardians of Shiʿism' (2015).

entries.label: Sectarianism institutionalised, then contested
entries.hint: The quota system wrote sect into the constitution and the state; the civil war of 2006–07 burned it into the map of Baghdad. And then the Tishreen generation, born into that order and sick of it, marched under the slogan 'we want a homeland' and explicitly refused sectarian identity as the basis of politics. Both things are true at once: the system runs on sect, and a growing part of the young rejects the whole frame.
entries.note: Fanar Haddad, 'Understanding Sectarianism: Sunni–Shia Relations in the Modern Arab World' (2020).

entries.label: The Sunni Arabs' predicament
entries.hint: The Sunni Arabs went from ruling Iraq to being a marginalised sixth of it. The insurgency, the exclusion by Baghdad, the alienation under Maliki, and finally the ISIS occupation and the destruction of Mosul, Fallujah, Ramadi and Tal Afar left the community shattered, displaced, and without a trusted leadership or a settled place in the political order. The Sunni question — how they belong in a Shia-majority Iraq — is still open.
entries.note: the ICG reports on Sunni politics in post-ISIS Iraq; Fanar Haddad on the Sunni predicament.

entries.label: The minorities' catastrophe
entries.hint: Twenty years undid two thousand of pluralism. The Christians fell from perhaps a million and a half to under a quarter of a million — the churches bombed, the Nineveh Plain emptied by ISIS. The Yazidis suffered genocide. The Mandaeans, the last gnostics, are all but gone from the rivers. The Kakaʾi, the Shabak, the Turkmen were all targeted. The tiny Jewish remnant of Baghdad is now counted in single figures.
entries.note: the reports of the Institute for International Law and Human Rights and of Minority Rights Group on Iraq's minorities; Sami Zubaida on Iraqi pluralism.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Iraqi novel comes into its own, the destruction and reconstruction of heritage, Mutanabbi Street and the cultural life, the media explosion and its capture, and the memory wars

entries.label: The Iraqi novel comes into its own
entries.hint: Freed from the censor, and driven by a subject no one could ignore, Iraqi fiction flourished — much of it written in exile and about the war and the dictatorship. Sinan Antoon's 'The Corpse Washer', Hassan Blasim's brutal short stories, and above all Ahmed Saadawi's 'Frankenstein in Baghdad', which won the International Prize for Arabic Fiction in 2014 by making the civil war into a monster stitched from the bodies of its victims.
entries.note: Ahmed Saadawi, 'Frankenstein in Baghdad' (2013, tr. 2018); muhsin al-Musawi, 'The Postcolonial Arabic Novel' background.

entries.label: The destruction and reconstruction of heritage
entries.hint: The Iraq Museum was looted in the days after the fall. Then ISIS made destruction a spectacle — the bulldozing of Nimrud and Hatra, the sledgehammering of the Mosul Museum, the blowing-up of the tomb of Jonah and, as it retreated, of the al-Nuri mosque and its leaning minaret. Since 2017 a slow reconstruction has followed: the museum reopened, the minaret being rebuilt, thousands of looted objects returned from abroad.
entries.note: the UNESCO 'Revive the Spirit of Mosul' programme; Benjamin Isakhan, 'The Politics of Cultural Heritage in Iraq' (2018).

entries.label: Mutanabbi Street and the cultural life
entries.hint: Mutanabbi Street, the old booksellers' row, was car-bombed in 2007 with some thirty dead — and rebuilt, its Friday crowds returning to the pavements piled with books. Through the worst years and out the other side the cultural life persisted: the theatre, the galleries, the music, the festivals, the cafés. By the late 2010s a cautious public space had reopened in Baghdad, and the young reclaimed it.
entries.note: the anthology 'Mutanabbi Street Starts Here' (2012); the reporting on Baghdad's cultural revival.

entries.label: The media explosion and its capture
entries.hint: After a single state channel, Iraq suddenly had hundreds of TV stations and papers — almost all owned by a party, a militia, a cleric or a foreign government, and pushing a line. Iraq became one of the world's deadliest places to be a journalist. The real reporting moved to social media, which carried the Tishreen protests and also a flood of militia disinformation and threats. The picture of Iraq stayed a contested space.
entries.note: the Committee to Protect Journalists Iraq data; the studies of Iraqi media ownership by the Institute for War and Peace Reporting.

entries.label: The memory wars
entries.hint: Iraq argues over its own past on many fronts: the Baʿth-era monuments kept or removed, the mass-grave memorials, the Speicher and Sinjar sites, the school textbooks rewritten every few years, the trials — of Saddam and his lieutenants, then of thousands of ISIS suspects in hurried hearings. There is no agreed account of the last half-century, and every faction has its martyrs and its villains.
entries.note: Eric Davis, 'Memories of State' (2005), on the background; the reporting on the ISIS trials and the mass-grave law.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The debate over what went wrong, the critique of the muhasasa order, the Najaf hawza and contemporary Shia thought, and the documenting of the atrocities

entries.label: The debate over what went wrong
entries.hint: The failed occupation produced a library: the memoirs of the officials, the reporters' books, the official inquiries — the Chilcot Report in Britain ran to two and a half million words — and the Iraqi accounts. The consensus that emerged names the same causes: the absence of a plan, the de-Baʿthification, the dissolution of the army, the reliance on exiles, the sectarian lens. It is the defining modern case study in how to destroy a state.
entries.note: the Report of the Iraq Inquiry (Chilcot, 2016); Ali Allawi, 'The Occupation of Iraq' (2007); Emma Sky, 'The Unravelling' (2015).

entries.label: The critique of the muhasasa order
entries.hint: Out of the protest movements — the 2015 electricity demonstrations, then Tishreen — came a political argument that rejects both the Islamist and the ethno-sectarian frames and calls for a 'civil', dawla madaniyya, state: citizenship instead of communal quota, competence instead of loyalty, accountability instead of consensus. It has no party of its own that can win, yet, but it has changed what a generation of Iraqis expects.
entries.note: the ICG report 'Iraq's Tishreen Uprising' (2021); Zahra Ali, 'Women and Gender in Iraq' (2018), on the protest politics.

entries.label: The Najaf hawza and contemporary Shia thought
entries.hint: With Iraq open again, Najaf reclaimed its place as the intellectual centre of Twelver Shiism, and its model — Sistani's quiet guidance, the marjaʿ as counsellor and last resort rather than ruler — stands as the implicit alternative to the Iranian doctrine of clerical government. The succession to the ageing Sistani, and the balance of authority between Najaf and Qom, are among the open questions of the Shia world.
entries.note: Sajjad Rizvi and Robert Gleave on Najaf and Sistani; Elvire Corboz, 'Guardians of Shiʿism' (2015).

entries.label: Documenting the atrocities
entries.hint: The record of the killings is being built grave by grave: the hundreds of Saddam-era sites, the ISIS pits at Sinjar and Speicher and Badoush, exhumed slowly for want of resources and law. A UN team, UNITAD, gathered evidence of ISIS crimes; the Yazidi survivor Nadia Murad, awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2018, made the genocide impossible to ignore. Accountability, for either era, is still mostly unfinished.
entries.note: the reports of the UN Investigative Team to Promote Accountability for Daʿesh/ISIL (UNITAD); Nadia Murad, 'The Last Girl' (2017).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The oil boom and the missing development, the public payroll and the private vacuum, the water and climate emergency, the corruption economy, and the Kurdistan boom-and-bust

entries.label: The oil boom and the missing development
entries.hint: Production more than doubled after 2009, to over four and a half million barrels a day, and the revenue has run into the hundreds of billions. There is almost nothing to show for it: the electricity still fails every summer, the roads and hospitals and schools are still broken, the young are still without jobs. The money is absorbed by a bloated payroll, fuel subsidies and theft. It is the resource curse at its most visible.
entries.note: the World Bank Iraq Economic Monitor; Ahmed Tabaqchali and the Iraqi budget analyses.

entries.label: The public payroll and the private vacuum
entries.hint: The state pays the salaries or pensions of a very large share of Iraqi households — the safest form of patronage — while agriculture and industry have all but collapsed and the shops are stocked from Iran and Turkey. There is no productive private sector to absorb the young, and no tax base to make the government answer for anything. The economy distributes rents; it does not produce.
entries.note: the World Bank and IMF Iraq assessments; Frank Gunter, 'The Political Economy of Iraq' (2013).

entries.label: The water and climate emergency
entries.hint: The Tigris and Euphrates now reach Iraq at a fraction of their old flow, dammed upstream in Turkey and Iran. The south is turning saline, the drought has returned, the dust storms come more often, and the Mesopotamian marshes — partly re-flooded after 2003 and given UNESCO recognition — are drying again. Water, not oil, may be the constraint that decides Iraq's next century. It is an existential threat, and there is no policy equal to it.
entries.note: the UN and World Bank climate assessments of Iraq; the reporting on the marshes and the Turkish and Iranian dams.

entries.label: The corruption economy
entries.hint: Iraq sits near the bottom of every corruption index. Estimates of what has been stolen since 2003 run past three hundred billion dollars — the ghost payrolls, the fictional projects, the party and militia control of ministries and border posts, and set-piece thefts like the 2022 disappearance of two and a half billion dollars in tax deposits. The state is widely understood, by those who run it, as a thing to be looted.
entries.note: Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index for Iraq; the reporting on the 2022 tax-authority theft.

entries.label: The Kurdistan boom and bust
entries.hint: The Kurdistan Region boomed from 2003 to 2014 — Erbil's skyline, the malls, the oil deals with the majors, the flights from Europe. Then the ISIS war on its border, the oil-price crash, and the punitive cut-off of the budget share after the 2017 referendum hit at once. Civil servants went months unpaid, the region ran up debts to its own oil traders, and the boom's promise faded into a grinding fiscal crisis.
entries.note: the reporting on the KRG fiscal crisis; Bill Park & others, 'The Kurdish Regional Government' in current-affairs surveys.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The reconstruction that mostly wasn't, the oil infrastructure rebuilt and expanded, the connectivity revolution, and the daily failure to keep the lights and the water on

entries.label: The reconstruction that mostly wasn't
entries.hint: Tens of billions in American, Iraqi and international money were spent on reconstruction — power plants, water systems, hospitals, schools — and much of it produced half-built or non-functioning projects, or nothing at all. The US special inspector's reports catalogued the failures: the security overheads, the corruption, the projects handed to Iraqi ministries that could not run them. It is a textbook of how not to rebuild a country.
entries.note: the reports of the Special Inspector General for Iraq Reconstruction (SIGIR), 'Hard Lessons' (2009).

entries.label: The oil infrastructure rebuilt and expanded
entries.hint: The one sector that got serious investment. The giant southern fields — Rumaila, West Qurna, Majnoon, Zubair — were developed by BP, Exxon, Shell, Lukoil, the Chinese majors and others under fee-per-barrel service contracts; the Basra export terminals were expanded; a common seawater-injection project long promised. The northern Kirkuk field and the pipeline to Turkey stayed tangled in the dispute with the KRG.
entries.note: the reporting on the 2009–10 licensing rounds; the Iraq Oil Report archives.

entries.label: The connectivity revolution
entries.hint: Under Saddam, satellite dishes were illegal and mobile phones essentially did not exist. Within a few years of 2003 Iraq had competing mobile networks and, before long, near-universal smartphones and social media. For a young population it became the medium of everything — organising the Tishreen protests, documenting the militias and the security forces, and carrying the disinformation and the threats back the other way.
entries.note: the ITU telecommunications data for Iraq; the studies of social media in the 2019 protests.

entries.label: The daily failure to keep the lights and water on
entries.hint: For twenty years the national grid has delivered a few hours of power a day in the summer heat, and the neighbourhood diesel generator — noisy, dirty, expensive — has filled the gap. The water-treatment and sewage systems remain broken; Basra's tap water turned toxic in 2018 and put a hundred thousand people in hospital. The everyday infrastructure failure is not a detail; it is the grievance that has repeatedly filled the streets.
entries.note: Human Rights Watch, 'Basra is Thirsty' (2019); the annual reporting on Iraq's electricity crisis.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Iraq between the United States and Iran, the regional dimension and the tentative return to the Arab fold, the pilgrimage and the transnational Shia world, the diaspora and the return, and the Kurdish region's foreign relations

entries.label: Iraq between the United States and Iran
entries.hint: The two powers that shaped the new Iraq have spent twenty years contesting it. The United States has a shrinking troop presence and heavy leverage over the banking system; Iran has the militias, the deepest ties to the ruling parties, a dominant trade position, and the religious and political networks. Every Iraqi government tries to hold the middle, and the ground shakes when the two collide — as in the Soleimani strike of 2020.
entries.note: Ranj Alaaldin and Renad Mansour on the US–Iran dynamic in Iraq; the reporting on the 2020 crisis.

entries.label: The regional dimension and the return to the Arab fold
entries.hint: After years as a pariah among the Arab states, Iraq has edged back: Saudi and Emirati re-engagement, a resumed border crossing and power line, the Baghdad conferences of 2021–22 that put Iraq briefly in the role of regional mediator between Riyadh and Tehran. Turkey keeps troops and airstrikes in the north against the PKK and controls the headwaters; the Syrian war spilled across the border and left it. Iraq is a bridge and a battlefield at once.
entries.note: the reporting on the Baghdad Conference for Cooperation and Partnership (2021, 2022); the ICG on Iraq's regional diplomacy.

entries.label: The pilgrimage and the transnational Shia world
entries.hint: The opening of Iraq reconnected the atabat to the whole Shia world: millions of Iranian, Gulf, Lebanese, South Asian and African pilgrims a year, the Arbaʿīn as a pan-Shia mass event, students returning to the Najaf seminary, and a set of financial and religious networks — the marjaʿ's representatives, the endowment flows, the media — that give Iraq a soft power it has not had in centuries.
entries.note: Elvire Corboz, 'Guardians of Shiʿism' (2015); the Arbaʿīn attendance figures.

entries.label: The diaspora and the return
entries.hint: Some of the exiles came home in 2003 to run the country — and were resented as 'suitcase politicians' who had missed the years of suffering. The emigration never stopped: a fresh wave to Europe in 2015, a steady brain drain of doctors and engineers, and the dual citizens who keep a foot in each world. The diaspora sends money, funds the parties, produces much of the culture, and votes with growing weight from abroad.
entries.note: the IOM and UNHCR data on Iraqi migration; Nadje Al-Ali & Zahra Ali on the diaspora.

entries.label: The Kurdish region's foreign relations
entries.hint: The Kurdistan Region runs its own foreign policy: a network of representative offices abroad, direct oil sales to Turkey, security cooperation with the United States, and a careful management of the KDP's Turkish tie against the PUK's Iranian one. The 2017 independence referendum tested it — and every outside power, even the friendliest, told the Kurds not to. The region acts internationally, within limits set by its neighbours.
entries.note: the reporting on the KRG's oil exports and the 2017 referendum; Bill Park, 'Turkey–Kurdistan Regional Government Relations' (2014).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The twenty-year war and its toll, the failed state that held, the Shia-majority Iran-adjacent Iraq, and the unfinished country

entries.label: The twenty-year war and its cost
entries.hint: The invasion, the occupation, the civil war and ISIS together killed somewhere between three hundred thousand and several hundred thousand more Iraqis, drove millions from their homes, levelled parts of a dozen cities, and traumatised a generation. It is one of the great catastrophes of the twenty-first century, and it followed directly from a decision taken in 2003 by governments that did not have to take it.
entries.note: the Iraq Body Count database; the several excess-mortality studies (Lancet 2006, PLOS 2013); the IOM displacement data.

entries.label: The failed state that held
entries.hint: Iraq was expected to break apart — into a Shia south, a Sunni centre, a Kurdish north — and it did not. The state is weak, corrupt and captured by parties and militias, its army has collapsed twice, its politics is a permanent bargaining crisis. But it has stayed within its borders through the civil war, ISIS and Tishreen. It is a country that functions badly and functions still, and has not, so far, come apart.
entries.note: Fanar Haddad, 'Understanding Sectarianism' (2020); Toby Dodge, 'Iraq: From War to a New Authoritarianism' (2012).

entries.label: The Shia-majority, Iran-adjacent Iraq
entries.hint: The strategic outcome of 2003 was the one Saddam's neighbours had feared and its planners had not foreseen: the removal of the Sunni-Arab state that had blocked Iran, and its replacement by a Shia-majority order run by Islamist parties with deep Iranian ties. The regional balance tilted; a land bridge from Tehran to Beirut opened; and the United States found it had fought a war whose main beneficiary was Iran.
entries.note: Vali Nasr, 'The Shia Revival' (2006); the strategic-studies literature on the post-2003 balance.

entries.label: The unfinished country
entries.hint: Twenty-three years on, the fundamentals are unresolved: a power-sharing system that cannot reform itself, an economy that only distributes oil money, a water crisis with no answer, militias the state cannot control, a Sunni question and a Kurdish question both still open, corruption near the world's worst — and a young population of some forty-five million, most of them born since Saddam, waiting for a state that works.
entries.note: the UN Iraq common country analyses; the World Bank Iraq systematic country diagnostic.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Muqtada al-Sadr, Ali al-Sistani, Nadia Murad, the Tishreen protester, and the internally displaced Iraqi

entries.label: Muqtada al-Sadr
entries.hint: A junior cleric of thirty in 2003, the son and son-in-law of martyred ayatollahs, he turned an inherited following of the poor Shia into the Mahdi Army, fought the Americans, and then built the largest bloc in parliament. Populist and mercurial, an Iraqi nationalist who denounces both Washington and Tehran, he leads mass marches, storms the legislature, quits politics and comes back — the pivot around which Shia politics turns.
entries.note: Patrick Cockburn, 'Muqtada' (2008); the reporting on the 2022 Green Zone crisis.

entries.label: Ali al-Sistani
entries.hint: Born in Mashhad in 1930, the senior Grand Ayatollah of Najaf since 1993, and the most consequential Iraqi of the post-2003 era — though he holds no office, gives no interviews, and is seen in public perhaps once a decade. He forced elections on the occupation, raised the volunteers who stopped ISIS with a single Friday sermon in 2014, and toppled a government in 2019 by withdrawing his blessing. Authority as restraint.
entries.note: the analyses of Sistani's interventions in Robert Gleave, Sajjad Rizvi and the ICG reporting.

entries.label: Nadia Murad
entries.hint: A Yazidi woman from the village of Kocho, near Sinjar, twenty-one when ISIS came in August 2014: her mother and six brothers killed, herself enslaved, sold and abused for months before she escaped. She chose to testify, publicly and repeatedly, and became the voice of the Yazidi genocide — the UN's first Goodwill Ambassador for survivors of trafficking, and, in 2018, a Nobel Peace laureate. The survivor as witness.
entries.note: Nadia Murad, 'The Last Girl: My Story of Captivity, and My Fight Against the Islamic State' (2017).

entries.label: The Tishreen protester
entries.hint: A young Iraqi born around 2000 — with a diploma and no job, no memory of Saddam, no stake in the parties that carved up the state — who came to Tahrir Square in October 2019 to demand a country: work, water, power, an end to the quotas and the militias and the foreign meddling. He faced sniper fire and gas canisters aimed at heads, and grenade-strapped drones. Six hundred like him were killed. Many of the rest are in exile or silent.
entries.note: the Human Rights Watch and Amnesty reporting on the 2019–20 protests; Zahra Ali on the Tishreen generation.

entries.label: The displaced Iraqi
entries.hint: One of the several million driven from home — a Sunni from a Baghdad neighbourhood cleansed in 2007, a Christian from the Nineveh Plain, a Yazidi in a tent at the foot of Mount Sinjar a decade after the genocide, a Turkmen from Tal Afar. Some went back to a ruin and rebuilt; some were resettled far away; hundreds of thousands are still in the camps, their towns unsafe or unclaimed, their return no nearer.
entries.note: the IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix for Iraq; the reporting on the protracted displacement after ISIS.
